Above that, in-house starts to win on cost and on responsiveness. The hybrid beats both in most cases: one in-house owner holding the CRM, the sales interface and the reporting, with media buying and creative production run externally.

### The cost comparison people get wrong
A competent performance marketer in Bangalore costs meaningfully more per year than most specialist agency retainers, and salary is the smaller half of the number. Add tooling, creative production, the months before they are productive, and the budget they will spend learning your category. The honest version is that in-house is not cheaper at low volume. It is better at high volume, which is a different claim.

### The split that usually works
One in-house owner, external execution. The in-house role holds the parts that cannot be outsourced — the CRM, the relationship with the sales team, and the authority to make them call leads inside 48 hours. Nobody outside your company can chase your own salespeople, and that chase is worth more than any optimisation. External handles media buying and creative production, which benefit from seeing many accounts and which do not require sitting in your office.

### The failure mode is identical in both directions
A marketing hire with no authority over sales follow-up, or an agency with no counterpart inside the business who owns the outcome. Both produce the same result: leads arrive, nobody is accountable for what happens next, and by the time anyone looks the launch window has closed. If you take one thing from this comparison, make it this — the appointment that matters is not who buys the media, it is who owns the number.


## AI creative volume vs studio production
URL: https://qdnco.com/compare/ai-creative-volume-vs-studio-production.html

VERDICT: AI-generated statics win on concepting, layout and the volume that real testing requires — bringing the marginal cost of a concept near zero changes which tests are worth running at all. Studio production wins, and is the only honest option, for anything depicting the actual property: the building, the elevation, the amenities, the view. Under RERA the promoter carries liability for what an advertisement depicts, so the project itself is photographed or rendered from approved plans, never generated.

### What actually changes
At studio rates, running six distinct concepts through three refresh cycles is a budget line most launches refuse. So campaigns run tired creative and blame the audience, and the refresh happens when a change order clears rather than when the numbers say so. Dropping the marginal cost changes which tests are affordable. The advantage is operational — more shots on goal, taken at the right moment — and it shows up in the account rather than in the artwork.

### The line, stated plainly
No AI-generated imagery of the project, the elevation, the amenities or the view. Layout, typography, background treatment, lifestyle context, copy — all fine. The building — never. This is not caution for its own sake. Under RERA the promoter carries liability for what the advertisement depicts, and "the tool generated it" is not a defence anyone has successfully run. A generated image of a building that does not exist as depicted is a misrepresentation risk sitting on the developer, not on the agency that produced it.

### How they actually work together
Test the argument cheaply, then produce the winner properly. Use generated statics to find which concept the market responds to — price, location, amenity, urgency, proof — across a real test with enough cells to kill a loser. Then commission the studio against the concept that won, with approved photography of the actual asset. That sequencing spends the production budget on a known answer instead of on a guess, which is the whole benefit.


========================================================================
# CATCHMENTS
========================================================================

## Real estate marketing in North Bangalore
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/north-bangalore.html
Corridors: Devanahalli · Yelahanka · Hebbal · Thanisandra · Jakkur · Bagalur · the airport corridor along NH-44
Delivered proof: This is the catchment behind our published benchmark: ₹266 cost per lead at a 51% sales-ready rate on a premium residential launch, with the quality rate scored by the client's own sales team.

### Who is actually buying
A materially larger share of investors than anywhere else in Bangalore, buying against future appreciation rather than immediate occupation. The airport, the metro extension and the employment corridors north of Hebbal are the underlying thesis, and buyers here are explicitly making a bet on timelines. That changes what a lead is. An investor enquiry has no urgency about possession and a great deal of interest in what the corridor will look like in five years, so the qualification conversation runs differently — intent windows are longer and budget bands are wider than the same ticket size would imply elsewhere.

### The argument that works
Connectivity and appreciation, evidenced. This is the one catchment where infrastructure timelines are genuinely the product, and where specific, checkable claims about them outperform lifestyle imagery. The corresponding risk is the one to manage carefully: infrastructure claims are promises about things you do not control. An advertisement implying a metro date or a road completion that slips becomes a complaint later, and under RERA the promoter carries it. Cite what is sanctioned and dated; do not imply what is merely announced.

### Why leads cost what they do here
North Bangalore during launch season carries one of the more contested ad auctions in the city, because a large number of projects are addressing an overlapping investor audience with a similar message. Cost per lead sits at the upper half of the ₹350–₹500 Bangalore residential band in most months. The ₹266 we delivered is below that band and should be read as what a well-targeted premium launch achieved, not as what the corridor costs generally.

### Language and targeting notes
English-dominant with meaningful Kannada uplift in the outer stretches towards Bagalur and Devanahalli. Worth split-testing rather than assuming; the assumption that everyone in the corridor reads English advertising quietly costs reach at the edges. NRI targeting is more productive here than in any other Bangalore catchment, and it needs its own campaign — different time zones, different creative, and a sales process that can handle a buyer who will not visit the site before booking.


## Real estate marketing in East Bangalore
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/east-bangalore.html
Corridors: Whitefield · Budigere Cross · Varthur · Sarjapur Road · Marathahalli · the Outer Ring Road tech belt
No published benchmark for this catchment.

### Who is actually buying
Salaried technology employees buying to live in, with the decision anchored to a specific office. The ORR tech belt and Whitefield campuses are the gravitational centre, and the catchment for any given project is drawn far more tightly than its postcode suggests — a project twenty minutes further out is competing in a different market, not a slightly worse one. The practical consequence is that the geography criterion in a qualified-lead definition does more work here than anywhere else. A lead from the wrong side of the ORR is not a marginal lead, it is a lead that will not visit.

### The argument that works
Commute, stated in minutes to named employers, and school access. Those two carry more weight than amenity lists in this catchment, and they are checkable, which makes them safe to advertise specifically. Ready-to-move and near-possession inventory has a structural advantage here that it does not have in North Bangalore, because the buyer has a lease ending and a date in mind. Under-construction projects in this corridor are advertising against a competitor the buyer can move into next month, and the campaign has to acknowledge that rather than ignore it.

### Why leads cost what they do here
High volume, high competition, and a large body of resale and rental inventory advertising into the same queries. This is the catchment where the Google negative keyword list matters most — "rent", "rental", "PG", "resale" and their variants will consume a search budget here faster than in any other part of the city. Cost per lead sits within the ₹350–₹500 band, with the wide variance driven mostly by how tightly the commute radius is drawn.

### Language and targeting notes
The most English-dominant catchment in the city, and the one where a multilingual split test is least likely to pay. It is also the most transient — a significant share of the audience has moved to Bangalore within a few years, which makes locality familiarity low and explicit orientation in the creative more valuable than it would be in West or South Bangalore.


## Real estate marketing in West Bangalore
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/west-bangalore.html
Corridors: Yeshwanthpur · Nagasandra · Peenya · Rajajinagar · Malleshwaram fringe · Tumkur Road along the metro
No published benchmark for this catchment.

### Who is actually buying
End users with existing family and community ties in the area, frequently buying within a few kilometres of where they already live, and often upgrading rather than entering the market. Business-owning and trading households are better represented here than in the technology corridors. This is the most important difference in the city and the one most often missed. The buyer already knows the locality — they do not need it explained, and creative that orients them reads as condescending rather than helpful. What they are evaluating is the specific building and the specific price.

### The argument that works
Value, clearly stated, and metro proximity in walking minutes. Price sensitivity here is genuine rather than performed, and a campaign that hides the price band to force an enquiry generates volume that fails the budget criterion at qualification. Publishing the entry price in the creative costs some leads and improves nearly every downstream number. In a catchment this price-sensitive, that trade is almost always correct.

### Why leads cost what they do here
Less contested than North or East, with fewer simultaneous launches addressing the same audience. Cost per lead tends to the lower half of the ₹350–₹500 band. The offsetting factor is ticket size. Lower average ticket means the same cost per lead consumes a larger share of the per-unit marketing budget, so the cost-per-lead advantage is smaller than it looks once expressed per booking.

### Language and targeting notes
The catchment where Kannada creative earns its place most reliably. A Kannada and English split test is worth running as standard here rather than as an experiment, and the uplift is usually in reach and cost rather than in conversion rate. Radius targeting also works better here than interest-based targeting, because the buyer genuinely is local — a tight geographic ring around the project outperforms a demographic profile drawn across the city.


## Real estate marketing in South Bangalore
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/south-bangalore.html
Corridors: Kanakapura Road · JP Nagar · Bannerghatta Road · Jayanagar · Electronic City fringe · Uttarahalli
No published benchmark for this catchment.

### Two buyers in one catchment
The established south — Jayanagar, JP Nagar and their surrounds — is old-money, premium, extremely locality-loyal and small in volume. The expanding south along Kanakapura Road and towards Electronic City is mid-market, price-led and high in volume. Running these as one campaign is the characteristic mistake here. The premium buyer is repelled by value messaging, the mid-market buyer is priced out by premium messaging, and a combined campaign optimises towards whichever fills forms more readily — which is the mid-market — while reporting a healthy cost per lead to a developer selling premium inventory.

### The argument that works, per segment
For the established south: locality permanence, build quality and the specific address. This buyer is not being sold on a corridor; they have chosen the corridor and are evaluating a building within it. For the expanding south: price, connectivity to Electronic City and the southern employment belt, and possession timeline. Closer in character to East Bangalore than to the premium pockets a few kilometres away.

### Why leads cost what they do here
This is the most contested auction in the city — the largest number of simultaneous advertisers addressing overlapping audiences, across the widest range of ticket sizes. Cost per lead is volatile and can exceed the ₹350–₹500 band during heavy launch periods. The practical defence is narrowness. Broad targeting in South Bangalore competes with everyone; a tightly drawn segment with a specific argument competes with far fewer advertisers for a much more relevant audience, and prices better despite the smaller pool.

### Language and targeting notes
Mixed, and it splits along the same line as everything else here. The established south is comfortably bilingual with strong Kannada resonance; the expanding south skews closer to the transient, English-dominant profile of the tech corridors. A single language strategy across the catchment will be wrong for one half of it. This is one of the few places where running two language treatments is worth the added campaign complexity.


## Real estate marketing in Mysore
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/mysore.html
Corridors: Mysore city · Ring Road corridors · Bogadi · Hunsur Road · Nanjangud Road · Bangalore–Mysore expressway belt
Delivered proof: Delivered cost per lead in Mysore and Tier-2 Karnataka has run at roughly half the Bangalore level, because the auction is far less contested. We publish this as a ratio rather than an absolute because it moves with ticket size.

### Who is actually buying
Three groups that need separating. Local end users buying to build. Bangalore-based buyers acquiring land as an appreciation play against the expressway. And returning or retiring buyers with family roots in the region. The second group is reachable from Bangalore and behaves like an investor; the first two are local and behave like end users. They justify different campaigns, and the Bangalore-based investor pool is the one most often missed because the geography targeting is drawn around Mysore.

### Trust, not lifestyle
Plot buyers here convert on clear title, approvals, boundary clarity and documentation far more than on rendered lifestyle imagery. The creative that wins in Bangalore apartment marketing frequently underperforms in this market for exactly that reason. Anything that reduces perceived transaction risk — approval status, survey clarity, plot dimensions, what is legally established rather than planned — outperforms aspiration. This is a market where the honest, document-led advertisement is also the better-performing one.

### The cost advantage, stated honestly
Roughly half the Bangalore cost per lead, against a slower sales cycle and a smaller absolute audience. Half the cost per lead with double the time to booking is not an improvement in cost per booking, and the arbitrage is only real for a project that can carry the longer cycle. More of the decision also happens offline and in person here than in Bangalore, which means the handover from marketing to sales matters more and a purely digital funnel will underperform its lead numbers.

### What the observed spend says
Our August ad snapshot includes plot and land advertising, but the retained buy-side set mixes geographies. It does not establish Karnataka-specific demand or profitability. Use local enquiry and sales evidence to validate the catchment. Public ad references can inform what to test; their recorded ages cannot prove which offers will sell.


## Real estate marketing in Tier-2 Karnataka
URL: https://qdnco.com/areas/karnataka-tier-2.html
Corridors: Tumkur · Hassan · Mandya · Ramanagara · Chikkaballapur · Doddaballapur · the expressway and highway belts
No published benchmark for this catchment.

### What transfers from the metro playbook
The mechanics do. Funnel structure, the separation of channel-partner and end-buyer pools, the qualified-lead definition, the CRM feedback loop and the budget floor all behave the same way, because they are properties of the platforms and of sales physics rather than of the city. The trust-led creative approach that works in Mysore transfers well across the region, and for the same reason: these are predominantly plot and land markets where the buyer is assessing transaction risk.

### What does not transfer
Audience size, relevance and expected event volume affect test design. A narrow catchment may produce limited reach or rising frequency; those observations need to be read alongside qualification and sales outcomes. Do not expand the geography merely to accumulate platform events. Broaden only when evidence supports an additional buyer catchment, then track those enquiries separately.

### What we do not know
We have not sized the developer population across Tier-2 Karnataka, and our market model explicitly leaves it out — the Bangalore figure is bottom-up and the Tier-2 addition is unsized. The cost arbitrage is documented from delivered work; the market depth behind it is not. So this page does not carry a benchmark, and any agency quoting you a confident Tier-2 cost per lead across the region generally is quoting a number they cannot support. The honest answer is that it is cheaper than Bangalore and that a specific project needs a specific read.

# RESEARCH

## 51 real estate marketing ads: a reproducible Meta audit
URL: https://qdnco.com/data/meta-ad-library-audit-bangalore-agencies.html
Published: 2026-08-09
Collected: 9 August 2026; counts reconciled 13 September 2026
Method: Recount of the retained Apify export. Group rows by the collector’s sell/buy label, deduplicate exact library URLs within each group, and count distinct advertiser display-name strings. The raw collection reports 204 items; 152 scored rows were retained. Three actors appear in the fallback log. Search terms and the source-file checksum are in the method download.
Sample: Sell: 56 retained rows, 51 unique ad links, 41 advertiser names. Buy: 96 retained rows, 96 unique ad links, 45 advertiser names. The combined retained set has 147 unique links.
Limits: Not a census of Bangalore agencies. CRM vendors are included; names are not verified legal entities or unique Page IDs. The export records one collection error. Search terms and collector labels constrain coverage; no agency websites were exhaustively audited. Retained run-age fields do not prove continuous delivery, spend, profitability or demand. The original raw 204 items are not all available in this retained export.

### What the retained data establishes
The August snapshot contains 51 unique sell-side ad links across 41 advertiser-name strings, plus 96 buy-side links across 45 names. Five duplicate sell-side URLs remain among the 152 scored rows. Counting rows as unique ads would overstate this retained sample. The collector labels describe how records were grouped for research. They do not establish that every seller is an agency, that every advertiser serves Bengaluru, or that every buy-side record is in Karnataka.

### Inspect the records and repeat the count
Download the 51-link sell-side index (CSV).Download the 96-link buy-side context index (CSV).Download search terms, counts, method and source checksum (JSON). Each CSV contains the snapshot date, collector category, advertiser name, library link, recorded ad age and matched search term. Ad copy, images, personal contacts and account credentials are excluded. Library links may change availability after the snapshot. To reproduce the index counts, count distinct library_url values and advertiser_name strings in each CSV. The JSON separately records the pre-deduplication row counts from the retained export. When the same link matched more than one search term, the first retained row supplies the displayed term and age.

### Activity is a starting point for questions
An advertiser’s continued presence can justify investigating its offer and creative. It cannot tell you whether the campaign produced qualified enquiries or bookings. The retained export has no spend, conversion or revenue fields. Compare the promise, destination, price presentation and qualification process against your own brief. Then test the relevant hypothesis in your own account with a defined lead-quality measure. A long-running ad is a research reference, not a proven winning creative.

### What we can say about transparency
This snapshot does not establish that no agency publishes prices, sells research or defines a qualified lead. Captured ad excerpts are not an exhaustive review of websites, proposals or commercial terms. Earlier wording made that unsupported inference; this revision withdraws it. Our own commitments remain concrete: published commercial terms, a documented research process and a written qualified-lead definition. Buyers can assess these directly without a claim that competitors lack them.

### How to cite or extend the audit
Cite QDnCo, the snapshot date, this page and the size of the relevant subset. Describe it as a keyword-selected snapshot. Preserve the distinction between rows, unique links and advertiser names. For a stronger follow-up, retain Page IDs, document geographic inclusion rules, review landing pages with dates and predefine the coding questions before collecting new records. That would support a different study; these downloads do not substitute for it.


## Bengaluru developer marketing: a transparent sizing scenario
URL: https://qdnco.com/data/bangalore-developer-marketing-market-size.html
Published: 2026-08-11
Collected: Q1 2026 source; model revised 13 September 2026
Method: Multiply ANAROCK’s reported Q1 launches by four; divide by an assumed 300 units per project equivalent; apply an assumed ₹1 lakh monthly agency fee for 12 months. A separate 50% selection scenario halves the result.
Sample: 24,400 residential units reported for Q1 2026. This is a launch-volume input, not a sample of agency contracts or an observed annual project count.
Limits: Quarterly activity may be seasonal. Unit counts include project phases and do not identify distinct engagements. Average project size, agency take-up, fee and engagement duration are unmeasured assumptions. The 50% selection factor is not a measured share clearing a budget threshold. Excludes existing inventory, non-residential work and other geographies.

### The sourced input and the correction
ANAROCK’s Bengaluru Q1 2026 Residential Market Viewpoints reports 24,400 launches. Read the original report for its coverage and rounding conventions. An earlier version used 27,000 from a search snippet. We replaced it with this directly checked report on 13 September 2026. The revised arithmetic below should not be combined with estimates from another provider without reconciling coverage.

### Calculate a scenario, step by step
With the assumptions below, the conditional fee pool is ₹39.04 crore; a 50% selection scenario gives ₹19.52 crore. Neither figure is a measured addressable or serviceable market. StepBasisScenario valueQuarterly launchesANAROCK Q1 2026 reported units24,400Four-quarter run rate24,400 × 4; assumes the quarter repeats97,600 unitsProject equivalents97,600 ÷ assumed 300 units325.33 equivalentsFee per equivalentAssumed ₹1 lakh/month × 12 months₹12 lakhConditional fee pool325.33 × ₹12 lakh; unrounded calculation₹39.04 croreOptional selection scenarioAssumed 50% take-up or eligibility₹19.52 crore

### Show how assumptions change the answer
Assumed units per equivalentEquivalent countFee pool at ₹12 lakh/yearAt assumed 50% selection200488₹58.56 crore₹29.28 crore300325.33₹39.04 crore₹19.52 crore400244₹29.28 crore₹14.64 crore A six-month engagement instead of twelve halves every fee-pool result. A lower fee or agency take-up reduces it again. These independent assumptions matter as much as project size; selecting only an optimistic combination would create false precision.

### What this helps you decide
Use the model to identify which inputs need field research: unique project and phase counts, in-house versus agency delivery, actual contract duration and fee distribution. A list of verified potential buyers is more useful for sales planning than the fee-pool headline. This model does not establish QDnCo’s obtainable revenue or prove that demand exceeds delivery capacity. Replace the assumptions with documented observations before using it for hiring or investment decisions.


## Real estate lead costs: reported examples and planning limits
URL: https://qdnco.com/data/real-estate-cost-per-lead-benchmarks.html
Published: 2026-08-11
Collected: Historical reports retained by August 2026; source status reviewed 13 September 2026
Method: Owner-reported figures retained in project notes. Illustrative cost per useful lead equals CPL divided by the quality rate. Underlying reporting periods, denominators and attribution need reconciliation before independently verified case-study claims can be made.
Sample: Selected examples, not a pooled or representative sample. The reported total engagement count is not the denominator for these CPL calculations.
Limits: The ₹266/51% example and enterprise portfolio report have different scopes. Enterprise experience may include execution through agency accounts and does not imply a direct developer appointment. Sales-ready is a historical label, not automatically the current contractual qualified-lead definition. No geography-wide or causal targeting conclusion follows from these examples.

### Read the source status with the number
ExampleReported figureSource status and scopePremium North Bengaluru residential₹266 CPL; 51% sales-readyOwner-reported; export and CRM reconciliation pendingEnterprise portfolio experienceApproximately 22,000 leads/month at ₹450 CPLOwner-reported portfolio-level experience through agency accounts; not a result for one named developmentBudget illustration₹350–500 CPLPlanning assumption; not an industry survey The first example gives about ₹522 per sales-ready lead by arithmetic. It does not establish the cost of a booking or collected revenue.

### Compare useful leads on consistent definitions
Illustrative comparison: ₹200 CPL at a 15% useful-lead rate gives about ₹1,333 per useful lead. ₹600 CPL at 60% gives ₹1,000. The lower raw CPL has the higher useful-lead cost in this example. Define the qualification criteria, duplicate window, reporting period and attribution method before comparing campaigns. Report the raw count and qualified count alongside percentages so small or incomplete cohorts are visible.

### Test the drivers instead of assuming them
Offer and catchment. Ticket size, location and buyer readiness can change both acquisition cost and conversion.Targeting. Broadening an audience may change volume and quality; the direction and size need to be measured.Optimisation and feedback. CRM qualification signals can support a downstream test when the integration and data quality are reliable. They do not guarantee an improvement.Follow-up. Contact speed, sales coverage and qualification consistency affect how many form submissions become useful conversations.

### Build a booking-cost scenario
For an illustration only, assume a 1% raw-lead-to-booking rate and ₹400 CPL. Ten bookings would require 1,000 leads and ₹4 lakh in media before agency fees and applicable taxes. At 0.5% conversion the same target requires twice the media; at 2% it requires half. Use completed sales cohorts to replace these assumptions. A recent lead cohort that has not finished its sales cycle cannot yet establish booking conversion.


========================================================================
# GLOSSARY
========================================================================

## CPL — Cost per lead
Total media spend divided by the number of leads generated. The most quoted number in real estate marketing and the least informative on its own, because it says nothing about whether the leads were reachable, in budget or in catchment.
At QDnCo: Working band for Bangalore residential is ₹350–₹500, moving with ticket size and catchment competitiveness.

## CPQL — Cost per qualified lead
The cost of a lead that meets a written qualification standard, rather than of any form submission. Distinguished from CPL by the fact that the qualification test is defined in advance and applied by the buyer, not the seller.
At QDnCo: QDnCo charges ₹550 per qualified lead, ₹495 above 60 a month, ₹450 above 120, with a 60-lead monthly minimum.

## Qualified lead
A lead meeting a pre-agreed, testable standard. Without a written definition the term means whatever the party using it needs it to mean, which is why disputes in this category almost always resolve to it.
At QDnCo: Five criteria: contactable within 48 hours across three attempts; budget inside the project band; intent within six months; valid catchment; not a CRM duplicate within 90 days.

## Sales-ready rate
The share of delivered leads that the client's own sales team judges worth pursuing after first contact. Multiplying CPL by the inverse of this rate gives the true cost of a useful lead.
At QDnCo: 51% delivered on a premium North Bangalore residential launch at ₹266 CPL — an effective ₹520 per lead worth working.

## Cost per site visit
Media spend divided by the number of prospects who physically visited the project. The most useful intermediate metric in real estate, because it is available within weeks and is much harder to game than a form fill.

## Cost per booking
Total marketing cost divided by units booked. The only metric that settles whether a campaign worked, and the slowest to become reliable because it waits on a full sales cycle.

## Lead-to-booking ratio
How many raw leads it takes to produce one booking. Varies enormously with ticket size, sales capability and lead source.
At QDnCo: Plan on 100:1 until your own sales data proves better — roughly 60% of raw leads qualify, and a strong team closes about 10% of those.

## Duplicate lead
An enquiry from a person already in the CRM. Charged twice by careless suppliers and a frequent cause of inflated volume figures.
At QDnCo: A 90-day CRM lookback is part of the qualification test, so duplicates inside that window are not billable.

## Lead decay
The fall in contact and conversion rates as time passes between enquiry and first contact. Steep in property, where a buyer typically enquires with several projects in one session.

## Replacement guarantee
A commitment to replace, free of charge, any lead that fails the written qualification standard, provided it is flagged within an agreed window.
At QDnCo: Seven days at QDnCo — short deliberately, so that leads are assessed while a fair assessment is still possible.

## Learning phase
A delivery-system learning period during which performance may fluctuate as the platform gathers events. Inspect tracking and lead quality throughout; the label is not a reason to ignore obvious problems or a guarantee of success when it ends.
At QDnCo: Review the current guidance for the specific platform and campaign type. Event volume, optimisation settings and recent edits matter; a learning label is not a universal currency-based budget rule.

## Optimisation event
The action an ad platform is instructed to maximise. Whatever you nominate is what the algorithm will find more of, which makes this the single most consequential setting in an account.
At QDnCo: A form-fill event measures form completion. A reliable CRM qualification signal can support a downstream optimisation test; it does not guarantee that the platform will find better leads.

## Optimisation floor
An informal planning term for whether a test can gather enough relevant observations for its intended decision. There is no universal rupee threshold established here for Meta or Google.
At QDnCo: QDnCo’s published working media minimum of approximately ₹1,00,000 per month is an engagement policy. Confirm the objective, event-cost assumptions, duration and spending cap for the actual test.

## Creative fatigue
The decline in performance that follows an audience seeing the same creative repeatedly. Diagnosed by rising frequency accompanied by rising cost per result.
At QDnCo: Frequency rising with cost means refresh the creative. Cost rising while frequency is flat means something changed in the auction — new creative will not fix it.

## Frequency
The average number of times each person in the target audience has seen the ad over a period. The leading indicator of fatigue.

## Instant form / lead form
A lead capture form that opens inside the ad platform rather than on a website. Produces more leads at lower cost and lower contact rates, because the friction that filtered out casual interest has been removed.
At QDnCo: Adding qualifying questions restores some of that filter. The friction is the point.

## Retargeting
Advertising to people who have already interacted with the brand — site visitors, video viewers, form abandoners. Cheaper per conversion than prospecting and strictly limited by the size of the audience feeding it.

## TOF / MOF / BOF
Top, middle and bottom of funnel: the three layers of a campaign structure, addressing people who do not know the project, are evaluating it, and are close to acting.
At QDnCo: Run with a fourth, separate retargeting layer, and with channel-partner and end-buyer demand as entirely separate pools.

## Attribution window
The period after seeing or clicking an ad within which a conversion is credited to it. Different windows produce materially different pictures of the same campaign.

## Last-click attribution
Crediting a conversion entirely to the final touchpoint before it. Systematically undervalues demand creation and overvalues demand capture.
At QDnCo: Why Google usually looks better than Meta in a naive report, and why cutting Meta on that basis tends to degrade Google a few weeks later.

## Negative keyword
A term that prevents a search ad from showing. In real estate the negative list is load-bearing, because the category is surrounded by rental, resale, PG and jobs queries that look adjacent and convert at zero.

## Brand defence
Bidding on your own project and company names in search so that others cannot intercept the demand you created.
At QDnCo: The cheapest traffic available. Left undefended, channel partners and aggregators will bid on your project name and resell you your own lead.

## Match type
How closely a search query must resemble a keyword before an ad is eligible. Broad match with a thin negative list is the fastest way to spend a real estate budget on irrelevant traffic.

## Ad set / campaign / ad
The three levels of a Meta account: campaign holds the objective, ad set holds budget, audience and placement, ad holds the creative. Budget and audience decisions live at ad set level, which is where most structural errors are made.

## CBO / ABO
Campaign budget optimisation lets the platform distribute budget across ad sets; ad set budget optimisation fixes it per ad set. CBO scales better; ABO gives cleaner tests because each cell is guaranteed spend.

## Meta Ad Library
Meta’s public ad-search resource. Our research index records ad links, advertiser names and reported ages from a historical collection. Those fields do not establish spend, continuous delivery, conversions or profitability.
At QDnCo: The retained 9 August 2026 export has 152 scored rows and 147 unique links: 51 sell-side links across 41 advertiser names, plus 96 buy-side links across 45 names. This is a dated snapshot; no continuous monitoring is implied.

## Lead routing
The rules that assign an incoming enquiry to a named owner. Leads arriving into a shared inbox, spreadsheet or WhatsApp group have no owner, and anything without an owner waits.

## Speed to lead
Elapsed time between enquiry and first contact attempt. The highest-leverage number in a property sales process and usually the least measured.
At QDnCo: Contactability inside 48 hours across three attempts is the minimum standard; median first-call times over 24 hours indicate a routing problem, not an effort problem.

## Feedback loop
Sending qualification outcomes from the CRM back to the ad platforms, so optimisation targets a downstream event rather than the form fill.
At QDnCo: Usually a few days of work and the highest-return technical task in a real estate funnel. Skipped more often than any other.

## Status model
The set of stages a lead moves through in the CRM. Fails when designed for reporting rather than for the salespeople who must maintain it — an unmaintained status model produces confident, wrong reports.
At QDnCo: Keep stages few and behavioural, and make the reason codes on "lost" mandatory. That field is where the marketing intelligence actually lives.

## Site visit
A prospect physically visiting the project. The first genuinely reliable indicator of purchase intent in residential real estate, and the point at which marketing hands over to sales.

## EOI — Expression of interest
A pre-booking indication of intent, usually with a small refundable amount, used to gauge demand before formal launch.
At QDnCo: An EOI campaign against an unregistered project is still marketing that project, whatever it is called.

## Channel partner
An independent broker or firm that introduces buyers in exchange for commission, typically 1–3% of unit value, paid on a closed sale.
At QDnCo: Not a competitor to performance marketing but a different instrument. Most developers should run both, with the attribution rule written down in advance.

## Attribution dispute
A disagreement over which channel caused a booking. Endemic where a channel partner introduces a buyer who first encountered the project through paid advertising.
At QDnCo: Settle it before launch with a documented introduction window and a CRM first-touch record as tiebreak.

## Client-funded media
An arrangement where the advertiser pays the ad platforms directly from their own account, rather than the agency buying media and rebilling it.
At QDnCo: The standard at QDnCo. It makes spend auditable without asking, and the account, its history and its pixel data remain the client's if the engagement ends.

## Retainer
A fixed monthly fee for an agreed scope, independent of results. Suits engagements where the constraint is the system around the leads rather than lead volume.
At QDnCo: ₹50,000–₹75,000 a month plus 8% of media and 2% on units above a written threshold.

## Performance fee
A fee tied to a delivered outcome rather than to time or activity. Only meaningful where the outcome has a written definition.

## Phase 0
A paid market diagnostic run before any advertising spend, covering buyer interviews, addressable demand, competitor and pricing analysis, and the campaign architecture.
At QDnCo: ₹75,000–₹1,25,000, two to three weeks. Structurally permitted to conclude that you should not spend — which research given away as pre-sales never is.

## Media under management
Total advertising spend an agency is responsible for across clients. A scale indicator, not a quality one.
At QDnCo: ₹6 lakh a month and above, client-funded.

## Influenced pipeline
The total value of sales opportunities a marketing programme contributed to, as distinct from revenue it can be said to have caused. Always the larger and softer number of the two.
At QDnCo: ₹37 crore across real estate engagements. Stated as influenced rather than closed, deliberately.

## RERA
The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016, and the state authorities constituted under it. Governs registration, advertising and disclosure for property projects in India.

## Section 3(1)
The provision prohibiting advertising, marketing, booking, selling or inviting persons to purchase any unit in a project that is not registered with the state authority.
At QDnCo: A hard gate. QDnCo does not run advertising for an unregistered project.

## RERA registration number
The identifier issued to a registered project, which must appear on advertising along with the authority's website address.

## Sanctioned plan
The building plan approved by the local authority. Advertising must depict what has been sanctioned — showing planned-but-unapproved amenities is the compliance failure that catches otherwise careful advertisers.

## Promoter
The person or entity developing and selling the project, as defined under RERA. Carries advertising liability — not the agency, the platform, or a channel partner who reposted the creative.

## Misrepresentation risk
Exposure created when advertising depicts something the project does not or will not have. The reason AI-generated imagery of the building itself is never used, however cheap it becomes.

## SEO — Search engine optimisation
Improving a page's position in the ranked list of results a search engine returns. Optimises a page against a query.

## AEO — Answer engine optimisation
Structuring content so an engine can extract a direct answer from it. The unit of optimisation is a passage rather than a page, which is why one question per URL outperforms one page answering eight.

## GEO — Generative engine optimisation
Getting a business cited inside AI-generated answers — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, AI Overviews — rather than ranked in a list of links. Rewards specificity, self-containment, consistent entity identity and original measurement.
At QDnCo: Near-duplicate content is the strongest negative signal available to it, and self-contradiction across a site is the second.

## llms.txt
A plain-text file at a site's root summarising what the organisation is and does, intended for language models and research agents rather than for browsers.

## Structured data / JSON-LD
Machine-readable markup embedded in a page describing what its content means — an organisation, a price, a question and its answer — rather than how it looks.

## Entity consistency
Whether a business is described identically across every source that mentions it — same name, address, phone number and claims. Inconsistency prevents an engine from resolving the mentions to one entity, so authority accrues to nothing.

## Citation (local SEO)
A mention of a business's name, address and phone number on a third-party site. Distinct from a link; the value is corroboration of the entity, not the link equity.

## AI Overview
Google's generated answer shown above the traditional results, assembled from multiple sources and citing some of them. Appearing in it is a GEO outcome, not an SEO ranking.

## Topical authority
The depth and coherence of a site's coverage of a subject, rather than the strength of any one page. Built by covering a subject completely enough that no obvious question is missing.
